pr_title: Portmapper improvements, and options to disable NAT
pr_body:
**- What I did**

- Allocate the same port for IPv4 and IPv6.
  - For example:
    - use the same ephemeral port for `0.0.0.0` and `::` in `-p 80`
    - use the same port for all addresses with matching port-mappings (same ranges and protocols):
      - `-p 0.0.0.0:8080-8083:80 -p '[::]:8080-8083:80'`
      - `-p 0.0.0.0::80 -p '[::]::80'`
      - `-p 233.252.0.2::80 -p '[2001:DB8::2]::80`
  - If the same port can't be allocated for all addresses, fail with an error.
  - If a host port is unexpectedly in-use, continue to look for an available port in the rest of the range.
  - fixes https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/42442
  - fixes https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/44136

- Add bridge driver option `com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=<nat|routed>` (and `com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv4=<nat|routed>`).
  - When set to `routed`, no NAT or masquerade iptables rules are set up.
  - The container is still firewalled, with an open port for each `-p`.
  - In `inspect` output, a non-NAT'd port mapping is shown with `"HostPort": ""`.
  - So, if the host's network has routing for a docker network, it's possible to communicate directly with the container's address.
  - _As with existing `-p` (`HostConfig.PortBindings`) options, a `--expose` (`Config.ExposedPorts`) for the container's port is still required to make the `-p` do anything. On its own, `--expose` doesn't result in the port being opened._
  - _Host address/ports in `-p` for a disabled-NAT network are ignored, the container's port is opened._

**- How I did it**

- Replaced the v4/v6 portmappers with (simpler) bridge code.
- Also moved the bridge-specific per-port iptables code into the bridge driver.

**- How to verify it**

New/updated tests.

```
# docker network create --ipv6 --subnet fdee::/64 -o com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=routed nnn
# netcat -l -p 8080   # make the first port in the range below unusable
# docker run --rm -ti --network nnn --name c1 -p 8080-8083:80 nginx
# docker inspect c1
[
    {
        ...
        "HostConfig": {
            ...
            "PortBindings": {
                "80/tcp": [
                    {
                        "HostIp": "",
                        "HostPort": "8080-8083"
                    }
                ]
            },
        "Config": {
            ...
            "ExposedPorts": {
                "80/tcp": {}
            },
        },
        "NetworkSettings": {
            ...
            "Ports": {
                "80/tcp": [
                    {
                        "HostIp": "0.0.0.0",
                        "HostPort": "8081"
                    },
                    {
                        "HostIp": "::",
                        "HostPort": ""
                    }
                ]
            }
}}]

# IPv4 has NAT rules ...
*nat
-A POSTROUTING -s 172.19.0.2/32 -d 172.19.0.2/32 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 80 -j MASQUERADE
-A POSTROUTING -s 172.19.0.0/16 ! -o br-c68a9a829188 -j MASQUERADE
-A DOCKER ! -i br-c68a9a829188 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 8081 -j DNAT --to-destination 172.19.0.2:80
*filter
-A DOCKER -d 172.19.0.2/32 ! -i br-c68a9a829188 -o br-c68a9a829188 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT

# IPv6 has no NAT rules ...
*filter
-A DOCKER -d fdee::2/128 ! -i br-c68a9a829188 -o br-c68a9a829188 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT

# docker-proxy for IPv4 only ...
# ps -ef | grep docker-proxy
root     11894 11420  0 15:08 pts/0    00:00:00 /usr/local/bin/docker-proxy -proto tcp -host-ip 0.0.0.0 -host-port 8081 -container-ip 172.19.0.2 -container-port 80
```

On a "CentOS 9 (stream)" VM, running firewalld, with addresses `192.168.175.43` and `fd48:70ba:de62:0:a00:27ff:fece:c637` ...
- created a network with no-nat for IPv6 as above (with IPv6 subnet `fd12:3456::/64`).
- Ran `firewall-cmd --reload`, checked that the rules were re-created.
- From another host, added a static route to the VM and checked that  `'http://[fd12:3456::2]'` and `curl 'http://192.168.175.43:8080'` worked as expected.

**- Description for the changelog**
```markdown changelog
- In port mappings with no host port specified, and with host port ranges, allocate the same port for IPv4 and IPv6.
- Add bridge driver option `com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=<nat|routed>`, when
  set to `routed` no NAT or masquerading rules are configured for port mappings.
  - This enables direct IPv6 access to the container, if the host's network can route packets for the
     container's address to the host. Mapped ports will be opened in the containers firewall.
  - For example, `docker network create --ipv6 -o com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=routed mynet`.
  - Option `com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv4=<nat|routed>` is also available.
```
pr_comments:
> All this talk about IPv6-mapped-IPv4 addresses is making me nervous. There is no semantic difference between listen()ing or bind()ing on [::ffff:10.0.0.1]:8080 vs. 10.0.0.1:8080. Only IPv4 packets will be accepted/transmitted over the wire for such a socket. So why does the portmapper need to fuss so much about `net.IP` slice lengths?

It needs to put rules into `iptables` or `ip6tables`, so it has to know what sort of address it's really dealing with.

I've added two commits ...

Improve PortBinding.String() - display port mappings in a format more like the CLI's, with all fields so that it's useful. This doesn't affect `inspect` or anything in the API.

Validate port bindings for gateway_mode=routed - when `-p` is used with `gateway_mode_ipv[46]=routed`, check that host IP/Port aren't specified. Previously they were ignored, but that could be misleading as, for example, `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` opened container port `80` for any traffic, it's not restricted to traffic originating from anywhere specific.

issue_context.title: port ranges: docker picks a host port used by process other than itself
issue_context.body:
### Description

Hello,

If I use a container port and map it to a range of host ports, docker picks one port from the specified host port range. 

When doing so, docker picks a port in-use by a non-docker started process, when there are other ports in the range that are available.

For example,
```
docker run -itd -p 21-23:100 busybox 
```
Above, docker would pick one of 21-23 host port and map it to container port 100.

In the same example above, lets say host port 21 is in-use by a running container, host port 22 is for ssh, host port 23 is available. Docker skips 21, but picks 22 and fails while trying to map it to container port 100. whereas, it should determine that both port 21 and 22 are in-use, and then pick port 23.

It seems to only know of ports used by itself (process called `docker-proxy`)

### Reproduce

1. check host ports in use, for example port 22 for SSH, etc.

(output below is just an example, not the entire list of ports on my host)

```
sudo netstat -tulpn | grep LISTEN

tcp        0      0 127.0.0.1:39097         0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      4824/containerd
tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      3479/sshd
```

2. run a container `ctr1` with 1 container port mapped to a range of host ports
```
docker run -itd -p 21-23:100 busybox 
```

port 21 is free, docker maps it to container port 100.

3. check in-use ports on the host

```
sudo netstat -tulpn | grep LISTEN
tcp        0      0 127.0.0.1:39097         0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      4824/containerd
tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      3479/sshd
tcp        0      0 0.0.0.0:21              0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      6105/docker-proxy   
```

4. run another container `ctr2`. 
```
docker run -itd -p 21-23:100 busybox 
```

this fails with reason:
`docker: Error response from daemon: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint X: Error starting userland proxy: listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:22: bind: address already in use.`

### Expected behavior

Docker should pick a host port that's not in-use, even if its used by processes other than `docker-proxy`

comments:
I started looking into this issue, but I'd like to gather insights from some maintainers to come up with a good way to fix it.

---

Port allocation starts here: https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/9052e33a10685a1f2188371624a08be2069889aa/libnetwork/drivers/bridge/port_mapping.go#L156-L167

Currently, if a port range (to pick from) is specified, then the loop early exits. This can be easily fixed (`if bnd.HostPort != 0 && bnd.HostPortEnd > bnd.HostPort {`) but I'm not sure about the whole design of portallocator & portmapper pkgs:

* The portallocator only iterates over the specified port range and checks if the chosen port is not already used by dockerd. It actually allocates nothing from the system.
* Then, the portmapper pkg starts either the userland proxy, or a dummy proxy. Both are the real thing allocating the port from the system.

I feel like the portallocator is wrongly named as it allocates nothing from the system. I'm considering changing that: portallocator would do the bind syscall and return the opened fd to the portmapper, so it can pass it to the proxy (if any). If the bind fails because the specified port is already used, it'd try the next port, and so on until it finds a port available. If we go along with this, I'd also remove the loop above as the portallocator would already implement the retry logic.

@neersighted and @corhere: What do you think about that? There seems to be an equivalent to SCM_RIGHTS on Windows, have you ever used it before? Have you other plans in mind about those two packages?
Hey, is this issue solved or is there any workaround to it?

Hi @ishaan1091, this issue is not solved yet and there's no workaround. However, I'm going to make important changes in the way the port allocator and port mapper work in the near future. Hopefully, it'll be fixed in v25.

Hi,
I believe I am having the same issue. What is the status of it?
Today I have updated Docker to v25, although from the [release notes](https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/25.0/), it seems this hasn't been fixed yet. If this is right, any idea of when it may be fixed?

> I feel like the portallocator is wrongly named as it allocates nothing from the system. I'm considering changing that: portallocator would do the bind syscall and return the opened fd to the portmapper, so it can pass it to the proxy (if any). If the bind fails because the specified port is already used, it'd try the next port, and so on until it finds a port available.

Genius, I love it! And it gets even better: we can ask the kernel to allocate a random ephemeral port for us by bind()ing to port 0! We'd only have to loop through ports if a user wants a different range for "container-ephemeral" ports than the kernel ephemeral range [and is not running Linux 6.3+.](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/ip.7.html#:~:text=IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE%20\(since%20Linux,the%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20lower%20bound.) The portallocator could become practically stateless! Although when it has to fall back to looping, the allocator should probably remember the most recent ephemeral port it probed [so it doesn't waste cycles always starting from the bottom of the range.](https://en.wikichip.org/wiki/schlemiel_the_painter%27s_algorithm) The portmapper (or userland proxy) would also need to keep a mapping of ip:port -> socket so it could release allocations, but that's about it.

> Port allocation starts here:
> 
> https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/9052e33a10685a1f2188371624a08be2069889aa/libnetwork/drivers/bridge/port_mapping.go#L156-L167
> 
> Currently, if a port range (to pick from) is specified, then the loop early exits. This can be easily fixed (`if bnd.HostPort != 0 && bnd.HostPortEnd > bnd.HostPort {`) but I'm not sure about the whole design of portallocator & portmapper pkgs:
> 
> * The portallocator only iterates over the specified port range and checks if the chosen port is not already used by dockerd. It actually allocates nothing from the system.
> * Then, the portmapper pkg starts either the userland proxy, or a dummy proxy. Both are the real thing allocating the port from the system.

Noting some findings from a rework I've got in progress ...

The existing code persists `types.PortBinding` objects from `Endpoint.portMapping` that represent allocated ports (operational state). In those, the `HostPort` is set to the port that was allocated but, `HostPortEnd` is not updated.

So, for example, for `-p 40000-40009:80` - if port 40004 was allocated, the stored binding would have `HostPort:40004` and `HostPortEnd:40009` ... so, it'd look the same as configuration for range `40004-40009`.

On live-restore, ports are restored using `Endpoint.portMapping` as configuration.

Continuing with the example, if some other process had grabbed port 40004 before dockerd tried to restore the mapping - because of the bug described by @akerouanton above, the apparent range would be ignored because `HostPort!=0`. When docker-proxy couldn't be started for port 40004, error handling would kick in. All of the endpoint's ports would be un-mapped, and none of its docker-proxy processes left running. It'd be quite hard to tell that had happened; the container would be running and connected to the network, with `docker inspect` showing the original mappings.

So ... a fix that adds `bnd.HostPortEnd > bnd.HostPort` to the retry test would result in mapping-retries happening on live-restore. Rather than no mappings, the live-restored service could end up with different mappings (and the original mappings would still be shown in `docker inspect`). That's differently and even-more-subtly broken, some mappings may work as-before and iptables and docker-proxy processes exist, it's only when comparing port numbers that the problem becomes apparent.

To keep the current behaviour, on reading `Endpoint.portMapping` from the store, `HostPortEnd` could be set to `HostPort`. (The `inspect` output could also be refreshed, to make it a little more obvious that the port mappings have failed. Better handling would certainly be possible though!)

`To4()` unmaps IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses but it's not called to assign `bnd.HostIP`. Maybe worth considering if that's not done upper in the call stack?
Yes, as I mentioned the other day, our handling of IPv4-mapped IPv6 isn't good. The behaviour hasn't changed, but I'll take a look.
Addresses are now unmapped early on - and added tests with IPv4-mapped IPv6 default-host, host, and container addresses.
The `dummyProxy` struct doesn't need to exist. Since it's started when constructed, the start function can be inlined and the stop function can simply be a closure which captures the listener.

As they're existing structs, and we may need to add an extra step in the initialisation - after binding, start accepting connections, to deal with https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/47871#discussion_r1624703022 - I don't want to go further down this route at the moment.
There's masquerading too, I generalised it as "NAT" in the comment.
Could you preserve this test while moving code to the `bridge` pkg? Or maybe don't move that code in the first place (see my other comment about that).

Splitting apart the DNAT/masquerade and filter rules is a main objective of this change, they're now controlled separately... so, the `Forward` function tested here no longer exists. There's better coverage in `TestAllocatePorts`.

This reminds me of the issue with `NetworkSettings.Ports` not being cleaned up when the daemon restarts/crashes and the container is already gone when `restore` is called. As a follow-up, I think we can add an `else` branch to zero out `Ports`.
Have you considered converting the implementation to use `net/netip` types internally, or would it be a bit much to tack onto this PR?
Yes, it'd be better - but also yes, a bit too much for this PR.

Huh? Why? It would make some sense in the `net/netip` world, where `netip.MustParseAddr("10.0.0.1") != netip.MustParseAddr("::ffff:10.0.0.1")`, but [the `net.IP` world makes no distinction between v4 and v4-mapped-v6 addresses.](https://go.dev/play/p/9zd6KA4Dget)
Because iptables vs. ip6tables.

ip(6)tables does not care either. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address is a transitional mechanism **for userspace** to be able to write dual-stack apps using only IPv6 APIs. A socket bound to such an address will transmit and receive IPv4 packets over the wire, be filtered by iptables (not ip6tables), etc. Do like the `net` package does and treat 16-byte IPv4 addresses as semantically identical to 4-byte IPv4 addresses. Use the idiom `isIPv4 := addr.To4() != nil` everywhere instead of `isIPv4 := len(addr) == 4` and there is no need to "unmap" anything, or risk bugs if addresses weren't unmapped in some code path or another. I would go so far as to advise _against_ unmapping `net.IP` values here so that any downstream code which incorrectly checks the slice length to determine address family behaves incorrectly in the common case.

An `iptables` rule with an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address will just-work. It's an IPv4 address.

An `ip6tables` rule with that address can be created, but it'll be useless because the packet it's aiming for will take the IPv4 route.

So, rules need to go into the right tables. The incorrect downstream behaviour you mention would be a bit invisible; the rule would be created normally, it just wouldn't do anything. I don't think that's something we want to invite.

There was one place where I compared lengths of addresses, knowing they were unmapped. It's gone now.
We're losing validation here, but since validation errors were never reported I guess it doesn't matter, right?
I renamed `validatePortBindingIPv4 ` to `configurePortBindingIPv4`, because that's what it does (and did). I don't think there's any less validation ... but, did you spot something specific?
The `proxyCommand` struct does not need to exist, either.
As above, for `dummyProxy`.
What's the reason to not make this call from the loop above?
Just that the iptables rules don't need to be set up if ports can't be reserved - this will change as iptables rules need to be set up first.
iptables rules don't need to be set up first, so this doesn't have to change. I don't think it needs to change, but can do?
Ah, fair enough! Let's keep it as is then.

I know that on Linux only the bridge driver uses this package, but honestly I'd prefer to keep both packages clearly separated to make sure we can easily test and evolve the portmapper. For instance, this would be helpful to add nftables support.

Also, looking at it, there are still some bits related to Linux like `StartProxy`, contradicting what the commit message says.

Generally speaking, it's better to not move code and evolve it at the same time. Otherwise it makes your life and reviewers' life harder (eg. when you have to rebase, etc...).

> I know that on Linux only the bridge driver uses this package, but honestly I'd prefer to keep both packages clearly separated to make sure we can easily test and evolve the portmapper. For instance, this would be helpful to add nftables support.

On Linux yes, only the bridge driver. But there's also Windows - which is almost completely different, but shared the same code. `bridge` had half of the bridge-specific iptables logic, with per-port logic living in `iptables`. We've discussed moving driver-specific logic into the driver several times, it's the right place for it.

The bridge's requirements have changed with the option to have no-NAT, iptables hasn't changed, but the implementation of forwarding/DNAT/masquerading etc was in `iptables.Forward` - behind two layers of indirection in the Linux & Windows `PortMapper` that would also both need to change.

`PortMapper` has a layer of indirection so that Windows can stub out most of the logic. If I'd made the changes in PortMapper, I'd have been changing the Windows code (which is hard to test and doesn't need to change yet, because it doesn't have IPv6 - when it does, the changes needed will inevitably be quite different to what was needed for Linux).

The `PortMapper` was also designed to deal with IPv4/IPv6 separately, which doesn't work.

So, `PortMapper` had to change. The best evolution for it is elimination - with `bridge` composing tools from `portallocator`/`iptables` and `portmapper` docker-proxy code directly.

In a first commit I called `iptables.Forward` directly from `bridge` code instead of indirectly through the `PortMapper`. In a second change I moved its bridge-specific logic into the bridge package - which meant using `bridge.iptRule` to be consistent with the rest of the bridge code. (`bridge.iptRule` itself isn't ideal but it can be improved separately, for all of the `bridge` code that uses it.)

> Also, looking at it, there are still some bits related to Linux like `StartProxy`, contradicting what the commit message says.

Right, the comment says "So, remove linux-specific portmapper code". It should be "So, remove linux-specific PortMapper code".

> Generally speaking, it's better to not move code and evolve it at the same time. Otherwise it makes your life and reviewers' life harder (eg. when you have to rebase, etc...).

Yes, agreed. But I think the alternative to what I've described above is not changing it, or making the messy Windows & Linux implementation more messy, so that it can still be used by both drivers to do quite different things. Is there anything specific I can do to improve things?

> Right, the comment says "So, remove linux-specific portmapper code". It should be "So, remove linux-specific PortMapper code".

Fixed commit message.

If the userland proxy was explicitly disabled and users ask us to bind an IPv6 host port to an IPv4 container port, I think we should explicitly error out. Is there any particular reason not to do that?

If there's no proxying and the container has no IPv6, it should error if ...

- the mapping has no host address, but the default address is IPv6.

Unrelated to this PR, but this makes me think... maybe we can now make 'hairpin mode' the default, or at least use it more often?

- Then, libnet devs realized the netlink message used was too new for some kernels supported at that time, as can be seen in this comment: https://github.com/moby/libnetwork/pull/412#issuecomment-124598326
- netlink uses the const `IFLA_BRPORT_MODE`, which was introduced by this commit https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/c75ea260400aaea8100caa012a0b1958ca094840, which was first released in v3.8.
- RHEL 8.10 uses 4.18 -- the oldest kernel we've to support. So we should be good by now.
- But we'd need to double-check if this would introduce new issues, etc...

I think you're right - but every other `'bridgeNetwork` method makes the same checks. A separate review/rework of all that could be good. But, for this change, it seems best to stick with tradition.
Nice! Done.
Since we already have a file `mapper_windows.go` in this package, I think it'd be better to merge them in a separate commit.

I considered that, but decided it'd be better to keep the git history for whichever file would go.

Also, the Windows portmapper will need a similar revamp anyway when we get IPv6 on Windows sorted out. So, most of it's likely to get deleted then anyway.
